A tutor is a person who teaches someone — but in a very personal, focused way. Unlike a school teacher who stands in front of a whole classroom of 30 students, a tutor works with just one person, or a very small group, giving their full attention to that individual's learning needs.

Think of it this way: a teacher cooks a meal for the entire family, using one recipe for everyone. A tutor cooks specifically for you — adjusting the ingredients, the spice level, and the cooking time based entirely on your taste.

A tutor's job is to help someone understand something better. This could mean:

  • Explaining a concept the student didn't understand in class
  • Practicing skills repeatedly with the student until they get it right
  • Answering questions in a relaxed, pressure-free setting
  • Spotting exactly where the student is going wrong and fixing it
  • Preparing a student for an exam or test

The key thing is personalisation. A tutor adjusts their teaching entirely around the one person sitting in front of them. If you don't understand something, they explain it again — differently. They have the time and the freedom to do that, because they're only focused on you.

1. Private tutors are the most common type. These are people — often hired and paid by a family — who come to a student's home, meet at a library, or teach online to help the student with their studies outside of school. A student who is falling behind in Maths, for example, might see a private Maths tutor twice a week.

2. University/college tutors (especially common in the UK and similar systems) are academics — often lecturers or senior students — assigned to a small group of university students. They meet regularly to discuss coursework, answer questions, and guide the students through their academic journey. Here, the word carries a slightly more formal, institutional meaning.

3. Peer tutors are students who tutor other students — usually slightly younger or less advanced ones. A senior student who helps a junior student understand Chemistry is acting as a peer tutor.

4. Online tutors do the same job as a private tutor, but over video call or through digital platforms.
How a Tutor Is Different from a Teacher

This is an important distinction.

A teacher works within a school system, follows a fixed curriculum, teaches large groups, and moves at a pace that tries to suit the majority of students. They can't always stop and give one student extra time — there are 29 others in the room.

A tutor, on the other hand, has no such constraints. Their entire focus is on one learner. They move at that learner's pace — faster if the student is quick, slower and more patiently if the student needs more time. There is no fixed script. The tutor shapes the lesson around whatever the student needs that day.

In short: a teacher delivers education to a group; a tutor tailors education to an individual.

• A tutor is not a babysitter — they are specifically there to teach.
  • A tutor is not always a professional teacher — many tutors are university students, subject experts, retired professionals, or knowledgeable individuals. What matters is that they know their subject well and can explain it clearly.
  • A tutor is not a replacement for school — they usually supplement formal education, filling gaps or strengthening weak areas.

The tutor-student relationship tends to be warmer and more personal than a typical teacher-student relationship. Because it's one-on-one, the student often feels more comfortable asking questions they'd be embarrassed to ask in class. There's no fear of looking foolish in front of peers. This safe, low-pressure environment is one of the biggest reasons tutoring is so effective.

• "She hired a tutor to help her son improve his grades in Science."
  • "My university tutor meets with me every two weeks to discuss my essay progress."
  • "He works as a private tutor on weekends, helping high school students prepare for exams."

A tutor is a person who teaches one individual (or a very small group) in a personalised, focused, and often private setting — adjusting their teaching entirely to suit that specific learner's needs and pace.
